START HERE / NO REAL MESSAGE NEEDED

Try three messages. Notice the difference.

Read the request first. Then compare it with the checker’s explanation.

Money request

“Move your savings to a safe account.”

Before checking: what would happen if you followed this instruction?

What to look for

The important clue is the request to transfer money to “protect” it. The secrecy instruction adds pressure. Use your bank’s existing contact details to verify a request like this.

Sign-in notification

“Your code is 123456. Do not share it.”

A code is mentioned, but no one asks you to send it to them. Does that distinction matter?

What to look for

Receiving a code differs from being asked to forward one. The deadline may still produce a weak signal. Consider whether you initiated the sign-in; a low score does not verify the sender.

Everyday deadline

“Urgent: bring your essay to class.”

The word “urgent” appears in an ordinary request. Should that word decide the result?

What to look for

A deadline alone is a weak clue. This example asks for an essay, rather than a password or payment. The checker should still explain the matched urgency wording instead of treating it as proof of fraud.

These are fictional learning examples, not an independent accuracy test. Analysis stays in your browser.

UNDERSTAND YOUR PROJECT

A checklist, a pattern model, and a points total.

Start with the plain-language answers. Open the technical details when you want more.

01 / READRead the pasted words and addresses.
02 / CHECKLook for specific requests and link clues.
03 / COMPAREFor eligible English texts, check learned SMS patterns.
04 / EXPLAINAdd signal points and show why they matter.
What do the rules look for?

Think of the rules as a checklist: is someone asking you to share a code, move money, keep a payment secret, or use an unusual address?

The request matters more than a single word. “Never share your password” differs from “Send your password to me.” The checks try to account for nearby wording, but can misunderstand it.

Technical details: rules and links

The rule checks use regular expressions, which describe text patterns. Normalization helps read fullwidth or invisible characters while keeping the matched text tied to the original message.

Link checks inspect hostname spelling and structure without opening the link. The small organization/domain list is incomplete. These checks do not authenticate a sender or scan files.

Source files: rules.mjs, text-utils.mjs, and link-checks.mjs.

Try explaining: why does receiving a sign-in code differ from being asked to forward it?

How are other languages checked?

Choose the message’s language. Spanish and Chinese starter rules look directly for requests such as sharing a code, moving savings to a “safe account,” or paying to unlock earnings. Both Chinese writing systems are included.

You can optionally translate into English on-device in a supported desktop browser, or paste your own translation. The English rules then check that wording as well. Findings tell you when their evidence came from the translation. Link addresses always come from the original message.

Translations can alter requests or negation. These multilingual checks have development tests, but no independent accuracy benchmark. The trained SMS model is skipped for all non-English and translated messages. Results and controls remain in English.

Technical details: local translation

The browser’s Translator API provides optional on-device translation. It may download language packs when you click Translate. No cloud translation API is called; the website does not upload the message. Feature detection handles browsers where translation is unavailable.

Native-language rules keep character offsets tied to the original message. English translation evidence has separate offsets and labels. The same signal only counts once across both texts. Source: languages.mjs, translator.mjs, and analyzer.mjs.

Browser translation documentation

How does the SMS model learn?

During training, it sees public text messages labeled “ordinary” or “spam.” It learns which word patterns occur more often in each group.

When you paste a short text, the saved model compares its wording with those learned patterns. Your message is not uploaded, used to retrain it, or remembered. Email uses the checklist rules only.

Technical details: TF-IDF and logistic regression

TF-IDF turns single words and adjacent word pairs into numeric features. Frequent words within a message count, and words common across many training messages receive less distinctiveness weight.

Logistic regression learns coefficients for those features. JavaScript combines the saved coefficients with the text features and compares the decision value with a threshold. A model match adds a supporting signal; its raw decision value is not a fraud percentage.

The model has 4,000 learned features and is limited to texts of up to 180 tokens with at least three known vocabulary tokens. Source: sms-classifier.mjs and sms-model.mjs.

Try explaining: what can a model trained on spam wording tell you, and what can’t it tell you about a sender?

What does the score actually mean?

The score is a total of warning points. A stronger request adds more points than a weak clue like a deadline. Related clues share limits, so repeating one tactic does not endlessly raise the score.

76/100 does not mean a 76% chance of a scam. It means matched clues contributed 76 points under this project’s scoring choices. Open the score explanation in any result to see the contributions.

Technical details: weights and limits

Each distinct signal has a base weight. Signals in the same family share a cap; some related signals therefore contribute fewer or zero additional points. The final total is capped at 100.

0–14 points shows few signals, 15–34 shows some concern, and 35–100 shows high concern. These cutoffs are design choices, not calibrated fraud probabilities. Source: analyzer.mjs.

Try explaining: why can a zero-point message still be a scam?

How do we know whether it works?

We check familiar scenarios, then separately measure performance on public messages the SMS model did not train on.

On the held-out English SMS set, the English detector flagged 94 of 100 spam messages and mistakenly flagged 8 of 700 ordinary messages. That leaves 6 missed spam messages. A mistaken flag is a false positive; a missed spam message is a false negative.

These are older SMS spam results. They do not establish how well the website detects modern phishing or email scams.

Technical details: training, validation, and testing

Training messages teach the vocabulary and model weights. Validation messages help select a decision threshold. Test messages are held back for the final evaluation rather than used to teach or choose that threshold.

Duplicates were removed and similar normalized templates kept in the same partition. The test set has 800 messages; authored practice scenarios are separate development checks, not independent accuracy evidence.

Recall is 94/100 = 94%: the share of spam flagged. Precision is 94/102 ≈ 92.2%: the share of flagged messages that were labeled spam. Ordinary-message false positives are 8/700 ≈ 1.14%. Source: MODEL_CARD.md and the research reports.

Try explaining: why isn’t the test-set recall a percentage chance that your next message is a scam?

Your first testing session: try the three guided examples, read one expanded explanation, and open its score breakdown. Keep a note of anything that feels confusing or incorrect; that feedback can guide the next improvement.

THE IDEA BEHIND SIGNALCHECK

Digital safety should
make sense to everyone.

A personal project exploring how explainable scam signals and a small, locally trained SMS model can help people check messages without giving up their privacy.

This prototype checks English, Spanish, and Chinese messages with request rules and original-link checks. An English-only SMS model also checks eligible English texts. Optional English translation runs on-device in supported desktop browsers or can be pasted manually. The interface and explanations are in English. It does not authenticate senders, scan attachments, or check live link reputations. It can miss scams and flag legitimate messages.

How the score works

Each distinct signal contributes a weight. Related signals share a cap so repeated pressure tactics or domain mismatches do not inflate the score. The total is capped at 100: 0–14 means few signals, 15–34 means some concern, and 35–100 means high concern. These weights are design choices, not fraud probabilities. A separate SMS model checks eligible short English texts for patterns learned from older spam examples; it is not used for email.

What we tested

On a held-out set of 800 public UCI SMS messages, the English detector flagged 94 of 100 spam messages and 8 of 700 ordinary messages. The first version flagged 8 of the 100 spam messages and none of the ordinary messages. Exact duplicates were removed and normalized message templates kept together before training, validation, and test splits. These are older SMS spam labels, not an estimate of modern scam or email accuracy. The separate 46 authored development scenarios are regression checks, not independent accuracy evidence.

SMS model data: Almeida & Hidalgo (2011), UCI SMS Spam Collection, adapted under CC BY 4.0. The model learns text features from the dataset; raw training messages are not included in the website.
